title: Mesolithic timbers survive 10,500 years beneath a German lake
dek: Worked posts and split boards found 20 metres underwater could rewrite what we know about hunter-gatherer construction in Central Europe.
body: Archaeologists diving in Lake Arendsee have recovered wooden posts and split boards bearing clear tool marks from a time when no farms existed in Central Europe. The timbers rest beneath roughly 20 metres of water in Saxony-Anhalt's Altmarkkreis Salzwedel district. State archaeologist Harald Meller said the finds shed a completely new light on the Mesolithic period, for which building traces in Central Germany have so far been known only as soil discolourations.

A post measuring about 1.6 metres tall shows apparent felling marks. Split boards reach up to 1.3 metres in length. Initial investigations suggest the pieces could belong to structures built by people living around the lake approximately 10,500 years ago. At that time communities survived by hunting, gathering and fishing. Project manager Marcel Weiß said determining exactly what the wooden remains represent could have important implications for understanding Mesolithic societies.

If evidence ultimately demonstrates permanent structures or intensively used living areas existed here 10,500 years ago, it would predate the arrival of the first farming communities and their longhouses in Central Europe by around 3,000 years. The exceptional preservation is linked to unusual geology. Unlike many inland lakes where sediment gradually accumulates, Lake Arendsee's bottom has been slowly subsiding due to geological processes associated with an underlying salt dome. This helped preserve parts of the ancient shoreline beneath a relatively thin sediment layer.

Researchers used a remotely operated vehicle equipped with high-resolution sonar to survey the submerged landscape and document the former shoreline contours. By recording the precise position of individual discoveries, archaeologists hope to identify concentrations of material that could indicate archaeological sites and determine where future underwater investigations should take place. Sven Thomas, diving operations manager for the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology of Saxony-Anhalt, said the support of underwater work with state-of-the-art technologies developed at the Fraunhofer Institute in Ilmenau is invaluable for archaeology.

Lake Arendsee has already produced finds from several periods including Neolithic fish weirs, a High Medieval flat-bottomed cargo vessel and a Late Medieval dugout canoe. The latest finds push the archaeological record beneath the lake considerably further back in time. Evidence already indicated people were present around the shores during the Mesolithic. The period is also associated in the region with the individual known as the Shaman of Bad Dürrenberg, whose grave has provided important evidence about Mesolithic life.

Archaeologists emphasise that investigations are continuing. Whether the timbers represent the remains of dwellings or another type of wooden structure is not yet known. Researchers are now attempting to establish whether the posts and boards formed part of huts, another type of construction or something not previously identified in the archaeological record.
doesnt_show: The finds do not yet show what kind of structures the timbers formed, whether they were permanent or seasonal, or how they relate to the broader Mesolithic settlement pattern around the lake.
settle: Detailed spatial mapping of the timber concentrations combined with further radiocarbon dating and microwear analysis would clarify the structures' form and function.
